newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole driving for election victory.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole driving for election victory.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole on Sunday were driving for victory in Tuesday's presidential election as polls showed Clinton with a shrinking but solid lead.
Republicans, however, seemed in an increasingly strong position to maintain control of both houses of Congress, leaving Clinton with a clouded mandate for his second term.
Dole resumed his unprecedented 96-hour around-the-clock campaign blitz on Sunday after a six-hour break in the California beach community of La Jolla to nap and clean up.

Clinton, clearly confident that he will win Tuesday's election, delivered sermon-like appeals for reconciliation, unity and votes in Florida, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Maine and New Hampshire, where many of the stops were more designed to help congressional candidates rather than himself.

Although he got a late start on Sunday, Dole resumed his hectic pace with a full slate of appearances in California, where internal polls showed him trailing by just four percentage points. The poll had a five-point margin of error.
"We are going to work around the clock, around the clock, around the clock," Dole told campaign volunteers in San Diego.

The 73-year-old veteran, defying his years and ignoring the need to sleep, addressed supporters in Omaha, Nebraska; Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Grand Junction, Colorado, and Las Vegas before making a pre-dawn landing in San Diego.
The Dole campaign was energized by poll data showing Clinton's edge narrowing after weeks of double-digit leads.
Although Dole's voice at times showed signs of strain, he continued to campaign enthusiastically. On Saturday, he added new stops to his itinerary, bringing to 19 the number of states on his route.
In an interview with ABC's David Brinkley, Dole said undecided voters were coming to him in the final hours of the marathon campaign.
"I think there's a big undecided vote," he said. "We're just now been getting an indication that the undecided are breaking in our favor."
"But the president's tough," Dole added. "Any incumbent president's tough. This president's a skilled orator. Good on rhetoric, short on programs, I believe."
Clinton aides said the president remained confident of his own victory and he struck a high-minded tone in his first event of the day at a black church in Tampa, Florida.
He later met with the mayor of St. Petersburg, Florida, scene of a riot last month after police shot a black youth.
Clinton said the choice before the voters on Tuesday was whether to build the nation's future on the "shifting sands of division or the strong rock of common ground."

"We will never be what we ought to be if we allow our country to be led by those who believe we are better off on our own, and who seek to pursue that path by driving wedges between us and exploiting our fears and convincing us that our brothers and sisters of different races, different faiths, different walks of life, are our inherent enemies," he said.
"That is a prescription for disaster," Clinton told the congregation at St. Paul's African Episcopal Methodist Church, where civil rights leader Martin Luther King once preached.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole within four percentage points of Clinton. ABC had the president 11 points ahead and Gallup put the president's lead at 13 points.

Individual state polls gave Dole some reason for hope. He was neck-and-neck with Clinton in Georgia and Tennessee, within five points in Ohio and led Clinton in Nevada -- all states Clinton carried in 1992.

Equally significantly, Republicans pulled ahead in the Reuters poll in the battle for Congress. The Republicans seized control of both houses in 1994 for the first time in 40 years. This year, they have been targets of an all-out assault by Democrats and their labor union allies.
The ABC poll showed that likely voters favored the Democratic candidate over the Republican in their congressional district by 53-42 percent, an 11 percent margin.
Most analysts now expect the Republicans to hold their own or even increase their majority in the Senate and to hold their losses in the House to a relatively small number.
